#10603. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

#10600. How to Organize CSS with Cascade Layers in Large Web Projects

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

As a website grows, its stylesheet often becomes harder to maintain. A rule added to fix one component can unexpectedly affect another, and developers may find themselves adding increasingly specific selectors to override previous styles. Over time, these changes make CSS difficult to understand and update.

CSS cascade layers provide a way to organize styles into named groups and control their priority. Instead of relying entirely on selector specificity and the order of declarations, developers can establish a predictable structure for their stylesheets.

CSS determines which declarations apply by considering factors such as origin, importance, cascade layer priority, specificity, and source order. When several rules target the same element, understanding these factors helps explain why one style overrides another.

If all three rules apply to the same button under normal author styles, the ID selector wins because it has greater specificity.

This can become inconvenient when a project contains third-party styles, reusable components, and application-specific overrides. Developers may respond by adding more specific selectors, making future changes increasingly difficult.

Cascade layers offer another approach: establish a clear priority order before writing individual component rules.

A useful starting point is to divide styles according to their purpose. For example, a project might contain reset styles, third-party styles, reusable components, and page-specific adjustments.

You can establish these layers at the beginning of your stylesheet:

The declaration at the top establishes the order for normal declarations in these layers. For normal author styles, later layers have higher priority than earlier layers, regardless of selector specificity between those layers.

This means a simple selector in a higher-priority layer can override a more specific selector in a lower-priority layer.

For more background on building adaptable interfaces, developers can explore SitePoint's introduction to CSS container queries, which explains another way to structure maintainable component styles.

Not every project needs the same number of layers. A small website may require only a few, while a large application may benefit from a more detailed structure.

This is a suggested structure rather than a mandatory convention. The important part is defining the priority order intentionally and applying it consistently.

Cascade layers can help avoid selectors that become unnecessarily complicated.

For normal declarations, the second rule wins because overrides has higher layer priority, even though the first selector contains an ID and more class selectors.

This can make changes easier to review because developers do not need to keep increasing selector specificity to achieve the intended result.

However, layer order should not become an excuse to place every exception in a global override layer. Keep related styles close to their components and use overrides only when the exception is intentional.

Cascade layers have rules that developers need to understand before adopting them across an existing codebase.

For normal declarations, later layers have higher priority. For declarations marked !important, the layer priority is reversed. Important declarations in earlier layers take precedence over important declarations in later layers.

Unlayered normal author styles also take precedence over normal declarations inside author cascade layers. This matters when integrating a layered stylesheet with older CSS that remains outside the layer structure.

The MDN documentation on CSS cascade layers explains these priority rules and provides additional examples.

Before reorganizing a production stylesheet, test how existing third-party rules, inline styles, and important declarations interact with the new structure.

Rewriting an entire stylesheet at once can introduce regressions. A safer approach is to define the intended layer order, migrate one group of styles at a time, and compare the rendered interface after each change.

Start with styles that are easy to isolate, such as resets or a small set of reusable components. Check buttons, forms, navigation, and responsive layouts at several viewport sizes.

Browser developer tools can help identify which declaration is winning and whether it belongs to the expected layer. Visual regression tests are also useful when the application has many shared components.

For teams, documenting the layer order and agreeing on where new styles belong can prevent the stylesheet from becoming disorganized again.

CSS cascade layers provide developers with a practical way to manage style priority in growing applications. By separating resets, vendor styles, components, and utilities into a clear hierarchy, teams can reduce specificity conflicts and make stylesheets easier to maintain.

The best results come from a deliberate layer structure, consistent naming, and careful testing during migration. Cascade layers do not remove the need to understand CSS specificity, but they give developers another tool for controlling how styles interact.

#10590. What Is the Best UI Testing Tool? 8 Tools Compared by the Job They Do (2026)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The ideal UI testing tool is the one that discovers what your users discover first: broken layouts, usability issues that no longer work, and new accessibility issues in all the browsers your users use before a change goes into the repository. In 2026, most frontend teams don't rely on a single tool to do all of that. The best setups involve two layers: a test runner layer that launches the browser and monitors behavior, and a UI testing and review platform that visually checks the outcome and routes changes to the right stakeholders for sign-off.

Even with the right stack, it still relies on what your team needs to catch. Different teams will focus on different points: a QA team trying to automate checkout flows, a design system team defending shared components, and a single developer working on a tight budget will all be somewhere different. This guide is categorized by the job these UI testing tools do, then connects them.

Most "best UI testing tool" lists rank test runners and visual testing platforms against each other as if they were interchangeable. They aren't. UI testing covers four distinct jobs:

Functional testing: Does the UI respond correctly when a user clicks, types, or hovers?

Visual testing: Does the UI still look right across layout, color, typography, and spacing?

Accessibility testing: Can people using keyboards and screen readers use it, and did this change introduce new violations?

Cross-browser and device coverage: Does it work in Safari on mobile, not just Chrome on a developer's laptop?

There are also other levels of UI tests. Unit tests test the logic but don't interact with the UI. End-to-end (E2E) tests represent the full user journey in a browser but are difficult to set up, hard to troubleshoot when the bug is a visual detail, and can't practically test every state. Between the extremes of unit tests and E2E tests, component tests simulate each component's behavior in a real browser using fixed inputs, offering speed closer to unit tests and user-level coverage closer to E2E. Many teams maintain a thin layer of E2E tests for critical journeys, and they have component tests for the dozens of states a component may be in.

These tools are organized by job so you can stack them rather than choose one winner.

Prices are taken from each vendor's site or published comparisons as of October 2026. Check current pricing before you buy.

These platforms sit on top of your test runner. They capture rendered UI, compare it to approved baselines, and give your team a place to review what changed.

Chromatic is a UI testing and review platform made by the Storybook team. It catches visual, interaction, and accessibility bugs in components and pages before they merge, and it gives developers, designers, and product managers one place to review UI changes and sign off. Chromatic's team is the core maintainer of Storybook, which has about 90,000 GitHub stars and 17 million weekly npm downloads, and a Vitest core maintainer on the team built Chromatic's Vitest integration. Chromatic is used by 45 Fortune 100 companies, including GitHub, Shopify, Microsoft, Adobe, the BBC, and monday.com

Pricing: Free plan with 5,000 snapshots per month (Chrome only), unlimited projects and users. Starter is $179/month for 35,000 snapshots and adds Safari, Firefox, and Edge. Pro is $399/month for 85,000 snapshots. Enterprise is custom, with SSO, SCIM, SLA support, and data retention. TurboSnap snapshots count as 0.2 of a regular snapshot.

Trade-offs: Chromatic is strongest when your UI is built from components. Teams with no component tests can start from Playwright or Cypress E2E tests, but they'll get the most value once components are covered too. Snapshot usage also grows with each browser and viewport you add, so plan coverage before you scale it.

Best for: Design system teams, product teams that want designers and PMs to approve UI changes, React Native teams, and Vitest-first teams that want visual testing without baselines stored in the repo.

Percy is BrowserStack's visual testing platform. It captures screenshots from your existing tests, renders them across browsers and responsive widths, and highlights pixel differences for review.

Strengths: Framework-agnostic SDKs for Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, and Storybook. App Percy covers native mobile apps. The free plan includes 5,000 screenshots per month with unlimited users and projects.

Trade-offs: Percy is page-oriented, and each page rendered in each browser at each width counts as a separate screenshot, so usage climbs quickly with cross-browser coverage. Percy compares feature branches against a base branch, which teams with complex branching should test early. Reviewers see rendered screenshots rather than an inspectable copy of the code under test, so debugging a diff usually means reproducing it locally.

Pricing: Free tier, then paid plans with fixed screenshot allowances and overage.

Best for: Teams already paying for BrowserStack that want visual checks on page-level E2E tests.

Applitools Eyes uses Visual AI to compare screenshots the way a person would, with match levels that can ignore content changes and focus on layout. Its Ultrafast Grid re-renders captured page states across many browser, viewport, and device combinations.

Strengths: Mature AI matching, broad browser and device coverage, Figma and Storybook testing, accessibility testing, and an MCP server. Higher tiers add AI-driven functional testing and plain-English test authoring.

Trade-offs: Applitools is priced and packaged for enterprises. There's a free trial but no free plan, and the Starter plan is $667/month billed annually for 100,000 component checkpoints or 1,000 page checkpoints. Professional and Enterprise are custom-priced.

Best for: Large QA organizations with big cross-browser matrices and budget for a dedicated visual AI platform.

Argos is an open source visual testing platform with SDKs for Playwright, Storybook, Vitest, and Cypress. It adds cloud baselines and team review on top of the screenshots your tests already produce.

Strengths: Simple flat pricing. The Hobby plan includes 5,000 screenshots per month, and Pro is $100/month for 35,000 screenshots, with a budget cap available.

Trade-offs: Argos focuses on visual diffs. Argos compares screenshots captured by your own test runs, so browser coverage depends on what your CI runs, and it doesn't offer hosted mobile simulators. It also has a smaller ecosystem than the larger platforms.

Best for: Small teams that want hosted visual review at a predictable price.

Test runners click, type, and assert. They're free and open source, and every platform above builds on them. On their own, they offer limited visual testing: built-in screenshot assertions store baselines in your repository, rendering can drift between laptops and CI, and designers have no review interface.

Playwright is Microsoft's open-source browser automation framework. It runs tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, with auto-waiting, trace viewer debugging and code generation, and supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.

Visual testing: Playwright's toHaveScreenshot assertion compares screenshots against baselines stored in Git. It works, but baselines must be regenerated per operating system, and accepting a change means rerunning with an update flag.

Best for: Teams automating critical user journeys such as sign-up, checkout and login. Pair it with a platform like Chromatic for visual review across real browsers.

Cypress is an open-source testing tool that runs inside the browser, with time-travel debugging that shows the app at each step of a test. It supports both E2E and component testing.

Visual testing: Cypress has no built-in visual comparison and relies on plugins or a platform such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools. Cypress Cloud, its paid service, adds recording, parallelization, flake detection and add-ons for accessibility and UI coverage.

Best for: Frontend developers who want fast feedback and an interactive test runner while they build.

Storybook is the open source workshop for building UI components in isolation. Each story captures one component state, and those stories double as test cases.

Testing features: Interaction tests with play functions and Testing Library, accessibility checks with the a11y addon, and a Vitest integration that runs stories as component tests.

Visual testing: Storybook doesn't diff screenshots on its own. Chromatic, built by the same team, is its visual testing and review layer.

Best for: Design system and component library teams, and any team practicing component-driven development.

Vitest Browser Mode runs component tests in a real browser instead of a simulated DOM, using Playwright or WebdriverIO under the hood.

Visual testing: Vitest's toMatchScreenshot assertion stores screenshots in the repository. For large projects, this can bloat the repo and baselines drift between machines. Chromatic can take Vitest Browser Mode tests with no code changes and run them in a stable cloud environment instead.

Best for: Teams already writing Vitest tests who want them to check how the UI looks without adopting a new framework.

Start from the problem your team is trying to fix:

"Shared component changes keep breaking other teams' screens." Test at the component level with Storybook or Vitest Browser Mode and Chromatic, so the change shows up on the pull request that caused it.

"Our Playwright tests pass, but the layout still breaks in Safari." Functional assertions don't check appearance. Add a visual testing platform that renders in Safari, such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools.

"We turned off screenshot tests because of false alarms." Look for deterministic component states and flake controls such as Chromatic's SteadySnap, or AI matching such as Applitools.

"Designers find UI bugs after release." Choose a platform with a review and approval workflow, and make sign-off a required pull request check.

"AI coding agents keep inventing components." Give agents access to your real component library, for example through Chromatic's hosted MCP, and run every agent-built change through the same UI tests as human code.

"We have no budget." Use Playwright or Vitest screenshot assertions, or start on the free tiers of Chromatic, Percy or Argos.

A practical, well-covered setup for a React web app looks like this:

Unit tests in Vitest for logic and utilities.

Storybook stories or Vitest Browser Mode tests for every meaningful component state, with interaction tests on key components.

Chromatic running visual, interaction and accessibility tests on those components in Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge on every pull request, with designers assigned as reviewers.

A thin layer of Playwright E2E tests for sign-up, checkout and other critical journeys, also captured in Chromatic so page-level visual changes go through the same review.

This keeps most UI coverage in fast, deterministic component tests, while E2E tests confirm the journeys that matter most still work end to end.

Playwright is the best free tool for E2E UI testing, and Storybook is the best free tool for testing component states. For visual testing, Chromatic, Percy and Argos all offer free tiers of around 5,000 snapshots or screenshots per month.

UI testing is the broad practice of checking that an interface works for users, including functional, visual and accessibility checks. Visual testing is one part of it: comparing rendered UI against approved baselines to catch unintended changes in layout, color, typography and spacing.

No. Chromatic was built by the Storybook team, but it also runs visual tests from Vitest Browser Mode, Playwright and Cypress tests, and from React Native Storybook on iOS and Android simulators.

Playwright's toHaveScreenshot covers basic visual checks, but baselines live in your repo, rendering can differ between machines, and there's no review interface for designers. Teams with several reviewers or many browsers usually add a platform on top.

Most teams use both. Component tests cover individual UI states quickly and reliably, while a smaller set of E2E tests confirms that critical user journeys work across the whole app.

#10588. How Healthcare AI's Early Wins Can Have A Lasting Impact

Dr. Paige Kilian, Chief Medical Officer at Inovalon, bridges clinical medicine and data analytics to improve real-world healthcare outcomes.

Everyone is trying to forecast AI’s effects on healthcare. Some believe it will finally free medical professionals from mundane administrative tasks so they can spend more time with patients.

Others worry it will erode the hands-on expertise required to deliver comprehensive, compassionate medical care. As AI creates the illusion of an easy approach to diagnosis, physicians will have fewer opportunities to learn by experience, potentially causing overreliance on technology at the expense of patient outcomes. Autopilot could not have landed Captain Sully’s plane.

Neither reflects what’s happening in most encounters today. Right now, physicians are overloaded with nonclinical tasks, patients are waiting too long for care and the playing field continues shifting as more regulations are announced and new technologies enter this space.

Fortunately, there are clear examples of AI catalyzing the change healthcare has long needed. I’ve observed them in my own day-to-day work. Models have produced exciting wins in taking on time-consuming, tedious tasks to help skilled experts make patient encounters more meaningful and, in some areas, produce better outcomes. AI scribes and other ambient documentation tools are giving physicians back time to focus on patients, and AI-based alerts are catching patient safety risks earlier.

The challenge is embracing innovation while preserving the art of taking the patient’s history, factoring in the nuance of expression and inflection and performing a solid physical exam; AI disruption has to happen in parallel to continued medical learning.

Forty-two percent of physicians report experiencing burnout, with administrative work as a primary contributor, a top reason why many physicians, nurses and pharmacists are leaving their professions.

Ambient AI can help ease documentation burden and give physicians time back to focus on patients. Doctors can turn away from the computer, look patients in the eye and still capture notes for later. For non-English-speaking patients, ambient AI could also be a valuable tool in improving communication with their providers.

The result is a more meaningful interaction without sacrificing the documentation accuracy needed to inform billing, quality measurement reporting and risk adjustment programs. In one study, clinician burnout fell 13% after 30 days of ambient use, and another study found that ambient scribes reduced cognitive load for physicians.

If agentic AI is added to providers’ toolkit, it can further offset administrative burden by helping appeal denials or complete prior authorizations. This is one area where early wins are signaling for healthcare teams to move faster. Thoughtful increased use of agentic AI can cut the costly inefficiencies taking up time and resources, allowing clinical teams to see their next patient sooner without sacrificing documentation needs for clinical care, quality reporting and prior authorizations.

In one study comparing AI-based recommendations for empiric antibiotics against what clinicians prescribed, the model chose the correct antibiotic as well as, or better than, the clinicians’ choices—and accounted for resistance profiles and chose narrower-spectrum antibiotics, reducing the risk of antibiotic-resistant infections.

In a cardiovascular health clinical trial, AI-enabled electrocardiogram (ECG) alerts reduced all-cause mortality rates within 90 days. AI alerts sent physicians a report of patients predicted to be at high risk of mortality, producing a 3.6% mortality rate in the intervention group compared to 4.3% in the control group. Separately, a systematic review of 11 randomized cardiovascular AI clinical trials found that five contributed to improvements in clinical events, six produced enhanced diagnostic accuracy and early detection and three yielded better resource utilization.

As AI is increasingly used in patient care, healthy skepticism must remain to prevent it from curtailing the experience on either side. Clinical experts still have to build their knowledge and apply best practices to each patient’s unique needs while also protecting patient comfort. AI might influence how they express themselves, making the combination of skilled medical practice and attuned bedside manner even more important.

For example, a patient who knows AI is transcribing their conversation may be less confident that the encounter is confidential. They might hold back or answer questions less honestly, and physicians need to catch these subtleties. AI can’t pick up if a patient isn’t looking their doctor in the eye or fidgeting while talking, yet these are the signals that create opportunity to foster connection and uncover important details about a patient’s wellness.

Clinicians must also prevent a diagnostic cascade. If doctors order tests based on AI recommendations, without performing a physical exam as well, one set of imaging could beget another test, more follow-up visits and potentially more invasive testing, which may not be warranted. Tests must be ordered based on sound clinical assessment, including an experienced physical examination that considers the patient’s unique history.

AI can’t replace decision-making in a particular encounter or in the years of practice required to build a personal medical perspective. Physicians must remain dedicated to their craft, with AI as a tool informing them in delivering care—and they should also consider how a patient’s behavior may change when they’re aware that AI is part of their care team.

The more AI takes on healthcare’s operational challenges, the more imperative it is for physicians to reinvest administrative time in continuing to sharpen their clinical skills. AI and human expertise need to progress together, with professionals staying committed to medical principles.

We’re seeing promising examples in lowering burnout and improving patient safety largely because the technology in these instances is taking on the complicated, task-heavy side of care and empowering clinical experts to focus on what the person in front of them actually needs. That’s the ultimate goal of AI use throughout the care journey: building highly skilled AI to collaborate with highly skilled humans to deliver the highest caliber, most compassionate healthcare possible.

Humans must remain at the controls of healthcare delivery, capitalizing on all the benefits technology offers while keeping it in an appropriate, clinical and caring context. There is no role for autopilot in the healthcare journey.​​

#10586. Hate hearing your own voice? Blame your skull

In the 20 years I’ve been a TV producer, media executive, and speaking coach, I cannot count the number of times I’ve seen people literally cringe upon hearing their own voice. Sometimes it’s a slight scrunch of the nose and sometimes it’s an audible sigh. Why do we hate our own voice? And what can we do about it?

It’s not you, it’s biology

You’re not that special. I don’t mean that rudely, but you’re actually a member of a very large club. The reason you hate the sound of your own voice is grounded in biology. In evolutionary terms, we have only been hearing our voice played back for a short amount of time. While humans have been around for hundreds of thousands of years, our recordings have not. Thomas Edison first recorded and played back his own voice just 150 years ago. (Fun fact: he sang “Mary Had a Little Lamb.”) Our body has not caught up yet to technology.

It’s your skull’s fault

Why do your friends not cringe at your voice, but you do? They hear your voice differently than you do. When we hear our own voice, there are vibrating sound waves hitting the ear drum and vibrations inside our skull due to our vocal cords. As they travel, the lower tones come through stronger. That makes us think our voice is deeper and richer than it is. When we hear our voice as it actually sounds, we’re not used to it.  

How to get over it

When you’re just starting to improve your speaking skills, it’s very hard to listen to recordings of your own voice. However, if you’re committed to improving, it’s essential. Every CEO I media train watches their TV segments back. Every coach I work with listens to the podcast they were a guest on. Every speaker I support watches their speech. We listen to it afterwards together. 

Familiarity breeds like

Familiarity often breeds liking because of a psychological concept known as the “mere exposure” effect. Listen to your voice back. I recommend starting with audio or video where you sound unrehearsed—on a zoom call or a friend asking you about something you love, like a hobby or a vacation. That way you’ll be hearing yourself as you actually sound.

Analyze it

Separate two aspects: your message and your delivery. Ask yourself: Do I like what I said in this video/segment/podcast? Then analyze it just for delivery. If this is too hard, read a transcript instead of listening to it. Now, listen to the recording. Listen for specific things, not a general “Ugh, my voice sounds weird,” which is unproductive. 

Ask yourself: Did I have vocal range? Did I use uptalk, ending my sentences like questions? Did I bring the right energy level? Your answers will point the way to improvement. If you are feeling particularly brave, you can send a sample to a friend or trusted advisor.

Voice memos are another great way to get more comfortable with the act of speaking on cue. You can send them to friends or clients. While you do this, use the wave form of voice memos or another app. Pay attention to your vocal range; you want a normal roller coaster, not high mountains.

Just because you are not used to your voice doesn’t mean there is anything wrong with it. The sooner you can move past the judgment around your voice, the sooner you can focus on what you’re saying and how you’re using your voice to spread your knowledge, be seen as a leader, or, well, just chat.

#10584. Midterm voters to decide on these key ballot measures, putting Trump’s agenda to the test

A battle over abortion rights is playing out in several states Tuesday as voters decide 145 proposed laws and constitutional amendments, including some that could affect voting for future elections.

The ballot measures provide a political undercard for a high-profile midterm election that will determine which party controls Congress, state legislatures and gubernatorial offices in many states.

Some measures put President Donald Trump’s priorities to a public test by gauging support for his attempts to reshape congressional districts, limit transgender athletes in sports and strengthen voter identification requirements.

Abortion ban faces an unusual redo in Missouri

Two years ago, Missouri voters became the first in the nation to pass a ballot measure undoing an existing ban on most abortions.

Now voters are deciding whether to repeal the 2024 abortion rights amendment and replace it with a new prohibition — this time allowing exceptions for medical emergencies and fetal anomalies, and in cases of rape or incest up to 12 weeks of pregnancy. The proposed ban was placed on the ballot by the Republican-led Legislature. Abortion rights advocates, led by national progressive groups, have greatly outspent abortion foes in a bid to defeat the measure.

In three other states, ballot measures would create a right to abortion using standards similar to what was in place nationally before the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022 and opened the door to state bans.

Ballot measures in Idaho and Nevada would block bans on abortion before fetal viability, usually considered after 21 weeks. Nevada voters already approved the measure once but have to do so a second time for it to become official. In Virginia, an amendment would ensure abortion is allowed for the first two trimesters.

Redistricting measures could affect 2028 elections

Nine states are using new congressional districts in the midterm elections after a rare spate of mid-decade redistricting encouraged by Trump.

Missouri’s Republican lawmakers also had adopted new House districts designed to help the GOP win an additional seat. But courts ruled they cannot be used unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. If passed, the districts would take effect for the 2028 election.

Voters in Democratic-led Maryland are deciding on a constitutional amendment that also could pave the way for new congressional districts in the 2028 election. Democratic proponents, backed by former President Barack Obama, have urged a “yes” vote as way to “stop Trump.”

Some Democrats also want to redistrict in Colorado. But a citizen initiative on the ballot would prohibit any potential 2028 redistricting from favoring one political party and require approval from both an independent commission and the state Supreme Court.

Transgender restrictions are proposed in several states

Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Missouri, Nebraska and Washington are considering measures restricting transgender athletes or medical procedures. That comes as Trump’s administration has been pushing for restrictions impacting transgender people, especially youth.

Most Republican-led states already bar transgender women and girls from female school sports teams. Citizen-led ballot initiatives propose similar restrictions in the Democratic-led states of Colorado and Washington. The Arizona measure would extend public school sports restrictions to private schools. And Nebraska’s measure would add existing restrictions to the state constitution.

A second ballot question in Colorado would ban some transgender medical treatments for minors. The Missouri abortion amendment also would add existing transgender medical restrictions to the state constitution.

Five state measures seek voter ID mandates

Though Trump’s push for nationwide voter ID mandates remains stalled in Congress, citizen activists bypassed Democratic-led state legislatures to place new voter ID requirements on the ballot in California, Colorado and Nevada.

Those measures would require government-issued identification — like driver’s licenses or partial Social Security numbers — to cast ballots. The Nevada amendment already won approval in 2024 but needs a second vote to take effect.

Measures referred to the ballot by Republican-led legislatures in North Carolina and Ohio would enhance existing voter ID requirements by placing them in the state constitution.

Six states consider citizen voting measures

Ballot measures in Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia would reinforce current election practices limiting voting to U.S. citizens.

Critics argue the measures are largely symbolic and unnecessary, because voting by noncitizens is rare and already forbidden in federal elections. But noncitizens are allowed to vote in some local elections in California, Maryland, Vermont and the District of Columbia.

Two years ago, similar citizen voting amendments won approval in all eight states where they appeared on ballots.

Elections themselves are up for a vote in some states

A Massachusetts ballot measure would end separate party primaries in favor of open primaries where the top two vote recipients of any party advance to the general election. In Alaska, voters are deciding for the second straight election whether to scrap their system of open primaries and ranked choice voting.

Proposed amendments in North Dakota and South Dakota would make it harder to amend their state constitutions by requiring 60% approval from voters instead of a simple majority. A similar 60% threshold is proposed in Utah for citizen initiatives that raise taxes.

Meanwhile, a Missouri amendment would make it harder for lawmakers to change voter-approved citizen initiatives by requiring revisions to get an 80% vote in the state House and Senate.

Colorado amendment would aid immigration enforcement

Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts could get a boost in Democratic-led Colorado under a proposed constitutional amendment that would chip away at state laws restricting cooperation with federal immigration agents.

The proposed amendment, placed on the ballot by conservative activists, would require law enforcement officers to notify the U.S. Department of Homeland Security when someone with an illegal or unknown immigration status is charged with a violent crime or faces a new charge following a prior felony conviction.

Arizona measure would limit traffic cameras

Voters in Arizona are deciding on a proposal limiting the use of traffic cameras to catch drivers speeding or running red lights. The Republican-led Legislature referred the measure to voters after Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vetoed a ban on the cameras.

Hobbs said the cameras enhance roadway safety, but opponents contend they infringe on people’s privacy and point to instances of misuse by certain law enforcement officers.

The proposal would bar new contracts for traffic camera systems starting in 2027 and require local governments to hold elections on whether to continue existing systems.

About half the states, including Arizona, have communities that use cameras to enforce speeding or traffic signal laws, according to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.

Associated Press writer Geoff Mulvihill contributed to this report.

—David A. Lieb, Associated Press

#10582. U.S. job postings rose sharply in September

U.S. employers ramped up their job postings in September as stronger economic growth may be encouraging more hiring. Yet voters are headed to the polls Tuesday, largely gloomy over an economy beset by higher prices.

U.S. job openings jumped to 7.5 million from a revised 7.19 million in August, the Labor Department reported Tuesday. It is the largest number of openings since May and up from a recent low of 6.9 million in March.

The department’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) also showed that gross hiring—job gains before subtracting people who quit or lost jobs—rose and layoffs fell in September.

The increases are a hopeful sign that hiring could improve, but the trend would have to continue for several months to suggest real progress. Hiring has been sluggish for nearly three years, though layoffs have also been historically low, a sign of meager “churn” in the labor market. Low churn means those who are employed are enjoying relatively high levels of job security, but it is much harder than normal for those looking for work to find a job.

Still, the number of job openings now exceeds the number of unemployed, a sharp switch from a year ago when there were more people out of work than available jobs.

“It’s an encouraging sign that despite all the headwinds right now with high diesel and gas prices and ongoing inflation problems, companies are slowly increasing their hiring,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said.

Job openings rose the most in professional and business services, which includes high-paying jobs in engineering and accounting, as well as jobs in the temp industry. Manufacturers, shipping firms, and state and local governments also advertised for more workers.

Nicole Bachaud, a labor economist at ZipRecruiter, cautioned that with inflation still high and interest rates having increased since the summer, companies may not be able to ramp up hiring by much in the coming months.

“All of that added up together just makes it much more expensive to operate as a business and much more expensive to expand,” she said. “And so that will likely continue to be a downward pressure on hiring, until we see inflation really able to cool down.”

The government will issue the October jobs report on Friday, which is forecast to show that employers added 65,000 positions last month, according to data provider FactSet. That would be an improvement from 29,000 in September. The unemployment rate is expected to stay at a low 4.2%.

Typically, job gains of just 65,000 would be seen as a sign of a struggling economy, but with the giant baby boom generation retiring and immigration sharply reduced, the economy doesn’t need to generate as many jobs as it has in the past for unemployment to remain low.

In September, layoffs fell sharply to just 1.64 million, the fewest since March 2025. The number of people quitting their jobs rose to 3.37 million, the highest in about 18 months, and up from 3.04 million.

The rise in quits is generally a good sign because workers usually leave a job when they either have another lined up or when they are confident they can find new work.

—Christopher Rugaber, AP economics writer

#10580. The Next Cyber Insurance Claim May Start With Authorized AI

Jay Bavisi is the Founder, Chairman, and Group CEO of EC-Council, a global leader in AI governance and cybersecurity education.

​In the current insurance landscape, underwriters know how to ask about stolen credentials, ransomware, unauthorized access, data theft and the controls that reduce those risks. That work is still needed. In fact, the cyber insurance industry has spent decades getting better at measuring compromise.

In a world where IBM’s “Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026” put the global average breach cost at $4.99 million, up 12% from the prior year, AI agents create a different level of exposure because a system can create material loss while using valid credentials, following an approved workflow and operating inside the authority the business gave it.​

Gartner predicts that by 2028, one-third of interactions with generative AI services will use action models and autonomous agents to complete tasks. As more of those agents move into business workflows, cyber risk will include what authorized systems are allowed to do when they are operating normally.​

Two companies can use the same model and carry very different levels of risk. One may only read information and recommend a next step. Another may send emails, approve transactions, modify customer records, change identity policies or call another automated system. For insurers, model choice is only part of the assessment. The authority attached to the system determines how a mistake becomes a loss.​

Every AI agent should have an authority budget, meaning the maximum set of consequential actions it can take without human approval. That budget should be visible to the business, the security team and, where the use case is material, the insurer. Nonhuman identities, OAuth tokens, API keys, service accounts and privileged access management will become financially relevant because they determine where the agent can go and what it can execute. More privilege means a larger potential blast radius, but more autonomy is not automatically more valuable.​

The question should be whether the marginal utility of giving an agent more authority justifies the additional exposure. If a recommendation produces most of the business value, allowing autonomous execution may add little utility while significantly increasing the consequence of failure.​

Recent cybersecurity evaluations show why this matters. OpenAI disclosed that models circumvented controls and reached external systems, including Hugging Face. Anthropic has separately reported Claude models gaining unauthorized access to real third-party systems during evaluations. These were not ordinary enterprise deployments, so they should not be treated as forecasts of future claims. They do, however, show how quickly capability, connectivity and permissions can combine once autonomous systems are given room to act.​

That creates a problem for static underwriting. An agent can gain new permissions, connect to additional systems or reveal new behaviors after a policy is bound. The annual policy may not have changed, but the authority budget has.​

An AI policy cannot show whether an agent’s authority is actually bounded. Before deployment, the approval process should connect the business case to the access being granted, the controls being tested and the human review that remains in place for higher-risk actions. This is where responsible AI has to move from principle to practice.​

The value of any framework depends on whether it helps teams document those choices in a way security leaders, boards and insurers can review. For insurers, that evidence may become as important as traditional security controls. A company should be able to show how machine authority was requested, approved, tested, logged and revoked as the agent’s role changes. Without that record, an AI policy says little about the risk created when an authorized system makes the wrong call.​

There are two questions I would urge all leaders to ask: What is the most consequential action our AI can take without human approval? Has that authority expanded since the risk was assessed?​

If the authority budget has expanded, the financial exposure has expanded with it. That is the point cyber insurance will have to absorb. In the agentic AI space, security posture is no longer the whole story. The ability to prove that machine authority is intentional, bounded, observable and reversible may become just as important to insurability as proving that the network itself is secure. That leads me to the main question we should ask: Can you tell me what your AI agent did last week?​

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

#10579. Election Day could mean big things for your 401(k). Here’s what history tells us

Whether or not Tuesday’s midterm elections deliver a so-called blue wave, one thing is for certain: More volatility will likely ripple through financial markets.

Midterm years have been historically weak for the U.S. stock market, delivering annual gains of just 7.5% versus an average return of 12.4% during non-midterm years, according to figures compiled by global investment management firm BlackRock. And even though more money has been pumped into this year’s midterm campaign than any other in history—to the tune of nearly $12 billion—your 401(k) portfolio isn’t likely to benefit so much.

Despite polling that points to Democrats gaining seats, nay the majority, in Congress, investors haven’t been positioning for such an outcome. Rather, a survey of more than 100 institutional investors conducted by Wolfe Research suggests that these key market players haven’t positioned themselves for any particular result, according to CNBC.

“Investors seem to have a significant dose of skepticism about whether the final outcome is going to be quite as favorable to Democrats as the polling suggests,” Tobin Marcus, the firm’s head of U.S. policy and politics, told the outlet. 

Likewise, veteran market strategist Ed Yardeni warns that the stock market hasn’t fully factored in a blue wave, as such an outcome could lead to “much worse” partisanship in Washington, D.C. “It could be a very cold shower for the market in terms of the gridlock,” Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, told Bloomberg. 

Why history favors investors

For long-term investors, the best course of action is to ignore election results and stay invested. BlackRock cautions that letting politics guide investment decisions has come at a significant cost in recent years. Since 2013, for instance, a $100,000 investment in the S&P 500 Index would have grown to nearly $400,000 at the start of 2026 if left untouched; by contrast, investors who moved money out of the market during that time frame based on their politics saw much lower returns.

What’s more, any kneejerk reaction to the election outcomes may not be as dire as some people are warning. 

JPMorgan’s trading desk puts the odds of a Democratic sweep at 66%, which would lead to a subdued knee-jerk response for the S&P 500. Instead, the less likely outcomes of Republicans retaining control of both the House and Senate (with odds of only 7%) or Democrats taking the House while Republicans maintain control of the Senate (with odds of 26%) could see stocks rise as much as 1.25%.

Any dips or spikes in the stock market are likely to be short-lived. Since 1970, the S&P 500 has risen by an average of 14.1% in the six months following midterm elections, according to BlackRock. However, in scenarios where one party lost majority control of both the House and the Senate—as polling suggests could happen this year—returns averaged just 10.4% during that same period.

HOW THE OUTCOME COULD AFFECT INVESTORS

Complicating matters for this particular midterm election is the sharp rise in stock prices this year, fueled by unprecedented spending to support the AI buildout. Meanwhile, the Treasury market just suffered its worst quarterly sell-off since 1994.

That’s meant a mixed bag for retirement savers as the classic 60/40 portfolio has delivered lackluster results this year. This allocation model, popularized by the likes of famed investor John Bogle, is made up of 60% stocks and 40% bonds. So far in 2026, the 60/40 strategy has delivered a return of nearly 7.1%, well below the 10.1% annualized return over the last 10 years, according to estimates by PortfoliosLab, a portfolio analytics and educational platform.

A Democratic sweep of Congress could put more pressure on stocks—and particularly the high-flying AI stocks that have driven most of the market’s rally this year. That’s because Democrats are seen as being more likely to pump the brakes on the data center projects that are crucial to the AI buildout and, hence, the market’s continued gains. 

Because of how central the AI trade has become to the overall market, investors will closely watch a few key governor’s races—particularly Texas, which Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has called the “epicenter of AI development.” A surprise loss for the incumbent governor has the “potential to spook” the stock market in the short term, as Wolfe Research’s Marcus told CNBC.

On the other hand, if Republicans somehow manage to retain control of both the House and Senate, it would have the most dramatic implications for the bond market, according to Reuters. That’s because the Republican policy agenda could continue, further expanding the deficit and therefore pushing Treasury yields even higher. 

But no matter what happens, Wednesday will at least bring an end to the deluge of political advertisements and texts to voters—as well as the pre-election anxiety that can grip markets, as Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at the wealth advisory network Carson Group, told CNBC. 

“Once you are through it, it’s a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well,” he said.

#10577. The next big subscription service could be sunlight. And it might cost $5,000 an hour

A startup wants to fill the night sky with ultrapowerful beams of redirected sunlight. What could go wrong?

According to astronomers, almost everything. Reflect Orbital’s plans to launch 50,000 satellites equipped with giant mirrors is akin to “a bullet in your head,” says one astrophysicist, citing threats to both the natural world and the future of astronomy.

Selling the sun

By offering “sunlight as a service,” Reflect aims to deploy a constellation of satellites to beam down 5-kilometer-wide solar rays on demand, ranging in brightness from “noon light to moonlight.”

Reflect’s website suggests potential use cases such as powering solar panels, illuminating disaster zones and search-and-rescue missions, and lighting up worksites, cities, and events. But with a price tag of $5,000 for an hour of sunlight, the product would be prohibitively expensive for most customers—leaving critics to assume that only militaries and titans of industry are likely to make use of Reflect’s services, despite its altruistic branding.

So far, Reflect hasn’t actually launched any satellites. In August, it received approval from the Federal Communications Commission to launch a single demonstration satellite (much to the chagrin of environmental groups, which urged the FCC to reverse its decision). But moving forward, Reflect won’t need to seek approval from the U.S. government at all: It recently booked two dedicated rocket flights with Skyroot Aerospace in India, which will be liable for any unintended consequences of satellites launched from within its borders under the Outer Space Treaty.

The end of astronomy

The prospect of messing with the day-night cycle immediately raised concerns with environmentalists and astronomers alike, who are already contending with an increasingly crowded night sky, thanks to spacecraft like SpaceX’s fleet of Starlink satellites.

Gáspár Bakos, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told Sky & Telescope that Reflect’s plans for “sunlight on demand” are “essentially ignoring all the progress we have made for the past many decades in bringing awareness to and decreasing light pollution.”

Bakos and other astronomers worry that the beams would cause light diffusion throughout the night sky, making it incredibly difficult for ground-based telescopes to view objects in space. Amateur astronomers would also be at risk of permanent eye damage if they happened to see one of Reflect’s beams through a telescope greater than 12 inches in aperture.

Lighting up dark environments at night could also pose a threat to plants and animals that depend on the day-night cycle for biological regulation. That includes humans, whose own circadian rhythms dictate sleep patterns, hormones, and digestion among other bodily functions.

Light bulb moment

In an interview with Payload, Reflect Orbital CEO Ben Nowack responded to frequent concerns about his company’s plans. If astronomers are concerned about light pollution, Reflect will be sure to avoid getting in the way of their telescopes, he reasoned.

“If there’s an astronomer or a place that doesn’t want to see light, and they have a really hard brightness requirement . . . we will make sure that we don’t serve customers close [by],” Nowack said.

As for anxieties around the impact of life on Earth, Nowack chalks them up to a general fear of new technology. “Similar concerns and fears were brought up when light bulbs were introduced to the world, and people were worried about circadian rhythm and, like, is this godly?” he said. 

Never mind the fact that Reflect’s beams of sunlight would be just a touch brighter than light bulbs, casting light for up to 30 kilometers from their targets. Each satellite would also appear in the sky as a point source four magnitudes brighter than the moon, according to a report by Bakos and his colleagues.

“This is not a ‘concern’—this is like a bullet in your head,” Bakos said. “It’s the end of ground-based astronomy.”

AI-generated images are becoming an important part of modern web development. Developers use them for website banners, product visuals, blog illustrations, backgrounds, and other digital content. However, creating an image is only the first step. Preparing it for efficient web delivery is equally important.

Unoptimized images can increase page size, consume unnecessary bandwidth, and delay page rendering. These problems can affect Core Web Vitals, especially Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), which measures how quickly the largest visible content element appears.

This guide explains how to optimize AI-generated images using practical techniques, including image resizing, modern formats, Node.js automation, responsive delivery, and performance testing.

Images often represent a significant portion of a webpage's total download size. When developers upload large images without processing them, visitors may experience slower loading times, particularly on mobile networks.

Large image files that take longer to download.

Incorrect dimensions for different screen sizes.

Missing image dimensions that cause layout shifts.

Excessive compression that reduces visual quality.

Unnecessary downloads caused by poor responsive configuration.

A consistent optimization workflow helps address these problems while maintaining the intended visual appearance.

Before preparing an image, determine where it will appear on the website. A full-width hero banner requires different dimensions from a product thumbnail or a small article illustration.

These are suggested dimensions, not fixed requirements. The actual size depends on the website layout and the devices being supported.

When preparing source visuals, developers can compare different AI image tools to understand how image generation workflows handle aspect ratios, output dimensions, and visual details.

Regardless of the generation method, keep an original high-quality version. This master file can be used to create smaller versions without repeatedly compressing an already optimized image.

Choosing an appropriate image format can reduce file size while maintaining acceptable visual quality.

AVIF: Provides efficient compression for many photographs and detailed illustrations.

WebP: Supports lossy and lossless compression, transparency, and animation.

JPEG: Remains useful for photographs and environments requiring broad compatibility.

PNG: Suitable for screenshots, lossless graphics, and images that require transparency.

No format is automatically the best choice for every image. Developers should compare the resulting file sizes and inspect image quality before selecting a format.

For technical details, consult the MDN Web Docs guide to image file formats.

Manually resizing multiple images can become time-consuming. Automation provides a consistent way to generate different image dimensions and formats.

Sharp is a Node.js library that supports resizing, compression, and image conversion.

The script generates WebP and AVIF versions at several widths.

The quality values are starting points. Adjust them after checking the output for compression artifacts, loss of detail, and unnecessary file size.

For additional configuration options, refer to the official Sharp documentation.

Responsive image delivery allows browsers to select an appropriate image based on available resources and screen layout.

The HTML srcset attribute provides multiple image candidates, while sizes describes the expected rendered width.

The browser uses the available image candidates and layout information to select a suitable resource.

Make sure the sizes attribute accurately reflects the actual website layout. Incorrect values can cause browsers to download larger images than necessary.

Responsive delivery is particularly useful when the same visual appears in different layouts across desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.

The HTML picture element allows developers to provide alternative image formats with a fallback.

The browser selects a supported source, while the img element provides fallback behavior and alternative text.

Always verify that the referenced files exist and that their dimensions match the intended layout.

Images without defined dimensions can cause page content to move while resources are loading. This can negatively affect Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

The browser can use the dimensions to reserve the appropriate space before the image finishes loading.

Images below the initial viewport can also use native lazy loading:

However, avoid lazy-loading the main hero image when it contributes to LCP. Important above-the-fold images should be loaded promptly.

Reducing file size should not significantly affect the visual details required by the website.

A practical quality-checking process includes:

Compare the optimized image with its original version.

Inspect the image at its actual display dimensions.

Test the output on mobile and desktop screens.

The smallest file is not necessarily the best option. A slightly larger image may provide noticeably better visual quality.

After implementing the optimization workflow, test the actual website rather than relying only on exported file sizes.

Open Chrome DevTools and select the Network panel. Filter requests by images and reload the webpage.

Mobile devices receive appropriately sized images.

The browser downloads unnecessary image files.

Modern formats are being served correctly.

You can inspect the image source selected by the browser using:

For websites containing multiple images, inspect each relevant element.

Finally, run an audit using Google PageSpeed Insights. It can help identify oversized images and other performance issues.

The web.dev guide to optimizing LCP also provides useful technical guidance for diagnosing loading delays.

Remember that image optimization is only one part of website performance. Server response times, caching, CSS, and JavaScript execution can also influence page loading.

Tinder has similar subscription tiers, with Tinder Plus and Tinder Gold offering perks like unlimited swipes and top picks for around $25 and $35 per month, respectively.

“Hinge is one of the highest-priced products we have. The revenue per payer, for example, at Hinge is almost twice that of Tinder,” Bailey said. “It also has one of the lower payer penetrations. Its payer penetration is only slightly more than half that of Tinder.”

The company did not respond to Fast Company’s request for additional details about the new subscription tier. 

The lower-priced offering comes as consumers grow increasingly frustrated with the dating ecosystem. In a February 2026 Harris Poll, 72% of Americans said romance feels more like a transaction due to dating apps, while 77% said dating has become a marketplace.

Despite those sentiments, Hinge’s monthly active user numbers are up 12% year over year.

While Tinder is still bigger, with around 8.9 million paid users, its base is shrinking, with its paid users down 4% from last year. Tinder has since leaned on a different strategy to keep users engaged, including facilitating in-person experiences to shift the focus away from swiping.

Match Group owns a number of major dating platforms in addition to Match, Tinder, and Hinge, including OkCupid and Plenty of Fish.

#10566. The Future Of Actuarial Risk Modeling Is Smarter, Not Just Faster, Computing

Sanchet Pachpute is CIO of New York Life Insurance Company, where he leads platform modernization for Institutional Annuities.

​For decades, actuarial modeling has operated under a constraint most of the business never sees: the sheer computational cost of understanding risk. Projecting and valuing a large insurance portfolio means running thousands of stochastic scenarios across a multi-decade horizon, accounting for mortality, lapse behavior, market conditions and regulatory reserve requirements at every step.

Done the traditional way, on a single machine working through calculations in sequence, that kind of analysis can take weeks. By the time the results land, the market conditions they were modeling have often already moved. This is a problem every carrier running sophisticated stochastic models eventually runs into, regardless of size or line of business.

In the past, how I’ve approached solving this is through high-performance computing: taking a workload built to run sequentially and rearchitecting it to run in parallel across a distributed cluster instead. In one case, a full valuation of a multibillion-dollar portfolio that took roughly 50 days of continuous sequential processing was rebuilt as a distributed workload and came down to roughly two hours. It was the same calculation and the same accuracy requirements spread across many machines working simultaneously, instead of one machine working through a queue. That’s close to a thousand-fold reduction in runtime, and it changes what the function can actually do day to day.

The architecture behind this kind of solution is, at its core, a straightforward idea executed with discipline: Break a massive computation into independent pieces, run them in parallel and reassemble the results efficiently. A coordinating process distributes scenarios across worker processes, each running its assigned share and streaming results back as it goes, with a final step combining everything into a portfolio-level answer.

None of the individual pieces are exotic. What makes this kind of system reliable in production is the discipline around it: fault tolerance so one failed worker doesn’t take down the whole run, careful memory management so dozens of processes aren’t duplicating the same reference data and verification steps that recheck a sample of results the traditional way. This confirms the parallel version hasn’t introduced errors nobody would otherwise catch.

The business impact shows up immediately in cadence. Valuations that used to run quarterly, because that was all the computational budget allowed, can run daily instead. Scenario coverage that used to be limited by time constraints can expand by an order of magnitude, which matters directly for tail-risk analysis. These include the rare, severe scenarios that conventional scenario counts tend to underrepresent simply because running more of them used to be computationally unaffordable. Going from 50 days to two hours doesn’t just save time; it converts actuarial modeling from a once-a-quarter batch report into an on-demand tool the business can actually iterate on.

Where this gets more interesting, and where I think most carriers haven’t caught up yet, is the next layer: using AI not to replace this kind of computing architecture, but to make it smarter about where it spends its cycles. Not every one of a thousand scenarios contributes equally to the final answer. Many cluster tightly around similar outcomes. Machine learning techniques can identify which scenarios are actually representative and which are redundant, letting a cluster spend its compute budget on the scenarios that materially affect the result rather than treating all of them as equally important.

Similarly, trained models can act as fast approximations for the most expensive parts of a calculation, with the full computation reserved for validation and for the scenarios where precision matters most. The computing architecture earns you the raw speed; applying AI on top of it earns you speed where it counts.

That second layer comes with a cost that’s easy to underweight in the excitement of the first. A faster model is only useful if you can still explain it to a regulator, and insurance is an industry where every material modeling assumption eventually has to be defensible, not just accurate on average. A surrogate model that approximates a reserve calculation needs validation against the full calculation on a meaningful sample, documentation of where it’s expected to be reliable and where it isn’t and a clear record of why it was trusted for production use. Skipping that step to chase speed is how a modeling shortcut turns into a regulatory finding 18 months later.

For technology leaders facing this same computational wall, the sequencing matters more than the headline speedup. Start with the distributed computing foundation and prove it against the existing process before trusting it. A 50-days-to-two-hours result only means something once the new system’s output has been validated against the old, slower one at scale.

Only after that foundation is solid should you layer AI-driven optimization on top, because AI applied to an unvalidated computation just produces unvalidated answers faster. Speed that your regulators and your own risk committee can’t fully stand behind isn’t actually an advantage; it’s a liability wearing the costume of one.

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

#10565. The 2026 midterm elections could change everything for Trump. Here’s what’s at stake

The midterm elections have the potential to upend everything from politics to business to the stock market. But the person most impacted by Tuesday’s results could be President Donald Trump, and that, in effect, could determine the course of his final two years in office.

On the political front, the battle to control Congress is key, with a number of seats in play, including 435 in the House of Representatives and 35 in the Senate.

Should the Democrats gain control of the House (and, perhaps, even the Senate), the voting public will have broken the Trump administration and Republicans’ stronghold over Congress.

“The midterms matter in general because they determine whether there is alignment between the executive and the legislative branches,” Harvard Business School professor Vincent Pons said in an interview earlier this year. “Oftentimes, voters vote against the party of the president. Some voters have a preference for divided government, to have checks and balances. If the Republican party was to lose the midterms, either the House or both the House and the Senate, it could have dramatic consequences in terms of circumventing the power of [the administration].”

A Democratic upset could check Trump’s power, paving the way for a lame-duck presidency for the remainder of his term. A blue sweep could also give Dems the votes they need to investigate the president’s finances, his administration’s immigration policies, and bring another impeachment.

In August, Michigan Democrat and Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed told CNN, “The first thing we’re going to do when [the Democrats] win this Senate seat? Hold Trump accountable. Then, on to the real work—taking on big corporations, taxing billionaires their wealth, and guaranteeing healthcare through Medicare for All.”

Back in January, Democratic Representative Micah Lasher of New York posted a road map for Congressional oversight should the Democrats regain control of the House: “Check the Trump administration’s lawlessness by making clear that illegal activity and corruption will be investigated, and by spurring criminal prosecutions or impeachments; focus the American public on the illegal and corrupt activity that gets lost in the daily barrage of news and distraction out of the White House; and shape the narrative of the 2028 elections and help Democrats win back the White House and grow our majority.”

In California, Democratic Representative Robert Garcia said he plans to look into the White House’s immigration policies, and “demand accountability” for the tactics used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement—the fallout of which would likely influence the 2028 presidential election.

In July, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat, said, “When you put us back in charge of the United States House of Representatives, you’ll get a Congress that speaks up for everyday Americans and a Congress that stands up to an out-of-control president.” Jeffries emphasized that to beat Republicans, Democrats were focused on healthcare costs, bringing down the high cost of living, and ending the war in Iran.

A divided Congress, with Republicans maintaining their majority in at least one branch, could result in major political gridlock for the remainder of Trump’s term, which could have major repercussions for business.

If Republicans can hold on to their seats, that could empower Trump to accelerate his domestic agenda and policies on key issues like defense and AI—with those government-connected sectors seeing continued growth, and banks and cryptocurrencies retaining lighter regulation.

#10564. AMVR’s new head strap is my favorite way to keep cool with a Meta Quest 3 or 3S

The upgraded AMVR BS1 head strap includes better ergonomics, a built-in fan, magnetic rechargeable batteries, and a new breathable mesh top support for ultimate comfort.

I don’t know how companies like AMVR and BoboVR keep doing it, but AMVR’s latest head strap is now the most comfortable cooling head strap I’ve ever used for the Meta Quest 3 and Quest 3S. If you’re still using the included cloth head strap or haven’t used a “cooling head strap” before, here’s how it works.

The AMVR BS1 uses a breathable forehead pad attached via magnets to the support bar. Inside that support bar is an adjustable-speed fan, which you can easily adjust using the recessed wheel on the right side of the head strap. This fan keeps sweat down and helps prevent lens fog, two problems that can be a constant annoyance.

The fan is powered by the magnetically detachable, rechargeable 8,800mAh battery pack that mounts on the back of the head strap, helping to even out the weight distribution across the headset. That battery pack will also charge your Quest while playing and adds around 4 hours of additional play time. You can always purchase more packs to keep things going for longer, if you need to.

Lots of padding can be found all around the headset, and the mesh support on top accepts any weight that remains. Every bit of padding is easily removable and washable, so you can keep things clean and tidy (especially if you share your headset with others). You can also get extra pads if you’d rather do it that way.

The back of the head strap cradles your skull with a mix of half supple padding and half grippy silicone. You’ll be double happy there, as the pad on the top part further cushions any headset weight, while the silicone keeps the headset from slipping forward and shifting weight onto your cheeks.

If you don’t need a fan, the BoboVR M3 Pro+ is currently $17 less than the AMVR BS1. I find the BoboVR M3 Pro+’s hybrid design to be slightly more comfortable, but the lack of a fan is a big negative for this particular BoboVR strap.

Once you’ve chosen a head strap, grab an AMVR FC4M face pad to add another layer of comfort to the headset. Like the AMVR BS1’s forehead pad, this face pad attaches to the Quest 3 (NOT the Quest 3S) via magnets and is made of breathable, easy-to-clean material. It’s perfect for staying cool year-round and makes the Quest so, so much more comfortable.
